name: Deandre Ayton
notes: Arizona's dominant freshman center, drawing David Robinson/Anthony Davis comps for a rare blend of a 7'5" wingspan, a 43.5" vertical and genuine footwork skill. Phoenix took him 1st. Ayton delivered real value early — All-Rookie First Team, a central piece of the Suns' 2021 Finals run and a franchise-record 64-win season — but was traded to Portland in the 2023 Damian Lillard deal, and a 2025 buyout amid reported discipline issues (tardiness, missed rehab) sent him to the Lakers and then Washington by 2026. Bust relative to a true No. 1 overall billing: real production and a Finals run, but never the perennial All-Star anchor the pick implied, and increasingly a well-traveled reserve.

name: Marvin Bagley III
notes: A reclassified five-star Duke freshman who dominated statistically (21.0/11.1 on 61.4% FG, ACC Player and Rookie of the Year), elite athleticism and rebounding the calling card. Sacramento took him 2nd. An All-Rookie season (14.9/7.6) suggested a real building block, but a relentless run of injuries — knee, thumb, foot — limited him to 13 games in one season alone, and a trade to Detroit followed by stops in Washington, Memphis, Dallas and Denver saw his production shrink to single digits. Bust: dominant one-and-done production undone almost entirely by durability.

name: Luka Dončić
notes: A 19-year-old Real Madrid starter who'd already taken over as primary shot-creator after Sergio Llull's injury — advanced ball skills, vision and shooting for his size, with lateral quickness on defense the honest question mark. Atlanta took him 3rd (traded to Dallas). Dončić delivered as thoroughly as any pick in modern draft history: Rookie of the Year, six All-Star and six All-NBA First Team selections by 2026, a scoring title and Finals run with Dallas (2024), a stunning 2025 trade to the Lakers, and a second scoring title (33.5 ppg) in 2025-26. Hit: a generational offensive talent whose only real question — defense — never stopped him from becoming a top-5 player in the sport.

name: Jaren Jackson Jr.
notes: A Michigan State freshman (Big Ten Freshman and Defensive Player of the Year, 3.0 blocks/game) whose defensive versatility was obvious even in a limited role off Tom Izzo's bench. Memphis took him 4th. Jackson's early seasons were injury-interrupted (a torn meniscus in 2020), but he developed into a genuine two-way force — leading the league in blocks (2021-22), the 2023 Defensive Player of the Year award, and multiple All-Star selections before a 2026 trade to Utah and season-ending knee surgery. Hit: the rim-protecting upside scouted at Michigan State became a genuine DPOY-level career.

name: Trae Young
notes: Oklahoma's historic freshman — the only player ever to lead Division I in both scoring and assists in the same season (27.4/8.7) — elite shooting range and passing paired with poor individual defense that scouts flagged explicitly. Dallas took him 5th (traded to Atlanta). Young delivered the offensive engine projected: multiple All-Star selections, a 29.6/9.3 All-Star-starter season, an All-NBA Third Team, and league leadership in combined points and assists (a feat matched only by Tiny Archibald) — before a surprising January 2026 trade to Washington on a $212M deal. Hit: the exact high-usage offensive engine scouted, defense remaining the permanent trade-off.

name: Mo Bamba
notes: A Texas one-and-done with a record-setting 7'10" wingspan and real shot-blocking/shooting flashes (12.9/10.5, All-Big 12 Defensive), but only one college season to judge overall polish and consistency. Orlando took him 6th. Bamba never turned the tools into a real role — bench-caliber production throughout (career 6.7 ppg across 368 games) and a string of trades (Lakers, 76ers, Clippers, Pelicans, Raptors, Jazz) confirming he never found a defined NBA fit. Bust: elite measurements that never became a translatable skill set.

name: Wendell Carter Jr.
notes: A five-star Duke freshman playing alongside Bagley (13.1/9.1/2.1 blk on 56.1% FG), strong rebounding and rim protection with three-point range (41.3%) as an encouraging bonus, ball skills still developing. Chicago took him 7th. A rookie-year thumb injury slowed the start, but a 2021 trade to Orlando unlocked a real role — a $50M extension, a 15.0/10.5 peak season, and a further $58.7M extension in 2024, remaining a steady rotation big through 2026. Solid outcome: a genuine, sustained NBA starter/rotation center, never quite an All-Star.

name: Collin Sexton
notes: Alabama's No. 2 point guard recruit nationally, an explosive scorer (19.2/3.6) whose ball-handling and playmaking volume were the flagged growth areas for a lead guard. Cleveland took him 8th. Sexton developed into a real high-volume scorer (a career-high 24.3 ppg in 2020-21) before a torn meniscus, then found a stable role in Utah (17-18.7 ppg) and later Charlotte, Chicago and, by mid-2026, the Lakers. Solid outcome: a genuine, sustained NBA scoring guard for nearly a decade, never quite the offensive engine his rookie pace suggested.

name: Kevin Knox
notes: A five-star Kentucky freshman and SEC Freshman of the Year (15.9 ppg), an athletic 6'8" scorer taken on pure shot-making upside from a thin one-and-done sample. New York took him 9th. A promising rookie year (12.8 ppg, Rookie of the Month) collapsed almost immediately — 6.4, then 3.9 ppg — and Knox bounced through six teams (Hawks, Pistons, Trail Blazers, Warriors) never regaining that rookie form (career 7.3 ppg across 320 games). Bust: an explosive rookie debut that never repeated.

name: Mikal Bridges
notes: A Villanova junior who transformed from a scoring recruit into a complete two-way "five-tool" wing (17.7/51%FG/43.5%3PT, Julius Erving Award), elite defensive versatility paired with real shooting. Philadelphia took him 10th (traded to Phoenix). Bridges became a defensive stalwart ("The Warden," All-Defensive First Team, a 2021 Finals run), then an offensive engine after a 2023 trade to Brooklyn (40-point games, 26.1 ppg stretch), and finally a 2026 champion in New York alongside fellow Villanova alums Jalen Brunson and Josh Hart — all while setting the NBA's active ironman streak (638 straight games through 2025-26). Hit: as complete a two-way value outcome as a 10th pick can produce.
